look_here_first: Like Texas snakeweed, an open and wispy yellow-flowering annual. Examine the back of a real flower head: pale/resinous phyllaries without green midnerve borders; then the DISC floret has long white basally united pappus scales, unlike G. texana's nearly absent/very short scales. Do not identify this species from habit/color alone; compare A. dracunculoides arrangement too.

key_traits.label: Family pattern
key_traits.text: Asteraceae composite heads: ray florets + disc florets inside a phyllary involucre, producing cypselae.

key_traits.label: Best field traits
key_traits.text: annual with broomy open branching; narrow alternate sessile linear leaves; gland-dotted aromatic foliage; many tiny yellow radiate heads; bell-shaped involucre with multiple phyllaries; calcareous soils and limestone outcrops

key_traits.label: Comparison training
key_traits.text: Compared with Amphiachyris dracunculoides, A. amoena is a Texas limestone specialist with very narrow sparse leaves and small resinous heads.

lookalikes.differences: Most important snakeweed double: both A. amoena and G. texana are open-panicle yellow-flowered annuals. A. amoena: whitish phyllary backs without green-lined midnerve and long spatulate-tipped DISC pappus scales, whereas G. texana has variable green-lined phyllary nerves and very short/absent pappus. Distinguish from A. dracunculoides with open versus crowded arrays and fruit rib count/receptacle hairs, not yellow rays.
